The fund owned some Lehman Brothers securities, and when Lehman filed for bankruptcy those securities lost value and Reserve concluded that its assets were worth only $0.97 per share. It had “broken the buck”; investors who had expected the fund to always be worth $1 per share were now disappointed. Investors demanded their money back, and Reserve had to close down, liquidate the fund, and give all of its investors back their money at a loss. Ultimately it paid them $0.991 per share. They lost 0.9% of their money. This was a huge scandal . It doesn’t seem that huge? But this was all quite rational. You see, if Reserve had cashed out all of its investors at $1 when they asked for their money back, the first investors to get cashed out would all get back $1 and have no losses, but eventually the money would run out, and the last investors left in the fund would get back $0 and have 100% losses. That’s what a bank run is. The last 0.9% of investors would have had 100% losses. The other 99.1% of investors would have been perfectly fine. In some abstract sense, if you were an investor in the fund, you had a 99.1% chance of being fine, so there was really no need to rush to get your money out. But because everyone knows the dynamics of bank runs , by backward induction, everyone had to demand their money back at once. So they did: “In just two days, redemption requests surpassed $40 billion ,” out of about $62.5 billion of asserts, and the fund had to shut down. The losses were not large . But tiny losses, combined with a very well-understood snowball effect, were fatal. Everyone could look several moves ahead, and what they saw, several moves ahead, was bad. Markets are efficient, so the bad thing immediately came true. Please take our quick reader survey . Bitcoin oopsie For a while last year, the US stock market would pay $2 for $1 of Bitcoin . It is hard to convey now how weird that time was. If you ran a tiny public company in mid-2025, the very best thing you could do was acquire $100 million of Bitcoin to add $200 million to your market capitalization. If you happened to have $100 million worth of Bitcoin in mid-2025, the very best thing you could do was to plop it into a tiny public company in exchange for $200 million worth of stock. These companies were called “digital asset treasury companies,” or DATs. Everyone kind of knew this couldn’t last ( it didn’t ), so there was a mad rush to get these trades done before the party ended. In September 2025, a company called Datavault AI Inc. got into this game. Sort of. Datavault was a small public company, “a leader in AI-driven data visualization, valuation and monetization.” In mid-September, it had about 116.7 million shares outstanding , trading at around $0.30 per share, for a market capitalization in the ballpark of $35 million. On Sept. 25, it announced that it was selling 278.9 million shares, at a price of $0.5378 per share, to Scilex Holding Co., another public company focused on “acquiring, developing and commercializing non-opioid pain management products for the treatment of acute and chronic pain and neurodegenerative and cardiometabolic disease.” [1] Scilex was paying the purchase price in Bitcoin, valued at $112,915.52 per Bitcoin , meaning that Datavault got about 1,309 Bitcoin for its stock. [2] The stock promptly shot up, hitting a high of $3.118 in October, for a market capitalization of about $973 million. Datavault did not, as far as I can tell, call itself a “Bitcoin treasury company” or DAT, and the announcement of the deal focused on its strategic goals, not the Bitcoin stuff. In writing a prospectus for a frontier artificial intelligence IPO, you have to make choices about what to promise in your good vision of AI, and what to threaten in your bad vision. SpaceX went public this year promising “the largest actionable total addressable market (‘TAM’) in human history,” $28.5 trillion, which is a lot, sure, but still a finite number of dollars. OpenAI has raised money to build artificial general intelligence with the considerably more abstract promise that “it may be difficult to know what role money will play in a post-AGI world.” So the two benchmarks are something like “we will make more money than any company has ever made before” and “we will make money obsolete.” Anthropic is, by these standards, relatively sedate. From its founders’ letter: We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history. As one of the companies at the very center of that moment, we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better. Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles. items.title: Money Stuff: Zuckerberg Wants to Keep His Votes
items.summary: Class C The basic deal is that if you found a company, and you want to raise money, you will probably have to give up some ownership of it. When the company is just you and an idea in your garage, you own the whole company. But if the company needs money to build factories or what have you, the people who give you the money will want something in return. Often what they will want is stock. If you hire employees, they will want stock. By the time your company is a big thriving public company, you might own only 10% or 20% of it. By that point, you might never again need to sell stock to raise money to do the company’s business. It’s thriving, it’s bringing in money, and if it is like the typical big US public company over the last few decades, particularly in the tech industry, it is bringing in more money than it needs to spend on growth. Until very recently , your company was more likely to be buying back stock than selling it. On the other hand, you might want money, for yourself. Maybe your yacht is getting a bit dingy, or you want to buy all the mansions around your mansion so no one can get too close to you. Probably you don’t have much liquid wealth other than the stock. So if you need a few hundred million dollars for yachts or mansions, the natural thing to do is to sell stock. But if you sell stock, you will own less of your company. You might, after founding the company and running it for many years and having your identity bound up with it, not like that. Well, tough. The thing that you have that has economic value is ownership of the company, and if you want to turn that into money you have to give up ownership. (Fine: You can borrow against your stock, which is not quite giving up ownership, though it creates some risk that you might have to.) There is a traditional compromise, which is that you give up some ownership but not control. Normally this is done with dual-class stock: Your shares get 10 votes per share, everyone else’s shares get 1 vote per share, so you end up with, perhaps, about 13% of the economic ownership of the company but about 60% of the votes. That way, you can pick the board of directors and run the company how you want, even while raising money — for yourself and for the company — from outside investors. If you sell some of your high-vote stock, it converts into low-vote stock, so you get money without giving up much control. You have to get your investors to agree to this, of course, and generally before you go public , but there is a long tradition of tech investors being fine with, and in fact liking , giving founders extra votes. [1] One minute, he’d be like “I want to make self-driving electric cars,” and another minute he’d be like “actually I want to colonize Mars,” and then he’d be like “I want to teach a monkey to play Pong with telekinesis ,” and then he’d be like “actually I want to make Twitter more right-wing,” and then he’d be like “I don’t like traffic so, tunnels.” And he was enthusiastic and persuasive and had a good track record of succeeding with kooky-sounding ideas, so you’d be caught up in whatever crazy-sounding thing he was telling you. If you had a billion dollars and happened to talk to him about that day’s enthusiasm, you’d give him the billion dollars to do the thing. In some sense, the billion dollars was not for brain implants or tunnels or Twitter or whatever; you were giving him the billion dollars as a bet on him , as a bet that whatever weird thing he touched he could turn to gold. But in another sense, the tunnels mattered; his enthusiasm for specific weird projects was contagious. Perhaps you found tunnels boring [2] but were really excited about brain implants, so you gave him money for some projects but not others. I don’t know that this was the dominant model, though. More likely , on Monday you gave him a billion dollars for space rockets, and then on Wednesday he came back to you and was like “I need a billion dollars for tunnels,” and you were like “oh, right, of course, the previous billion dollars was for the rockets, I can see why you’d need a different pot of money for the tunnels.” In any case, by doing all the different projects in different companies with (possibly) different investors, he maximized his fundraising surface area. All of his investors got concentrated high-upside bets on whatever the relevant enthusiasm was. And then he went and did all of the things. There were some conflicts of interest involved in having one guy run all these companies doing all of these things.
